title: MC1-08227
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): These are my reasons for dismissing the appeal of XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellant) and confirming the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) that he is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: These are my reasons for dismissing the appeal of XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellant) and confirming the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) that he is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection.

The Appellant is a citizen of Nigeria from Ondo State. He alleges that his uncle, A.,1 has threatened to kill him due to a land dispute over his late father's property. He alleges that A. was unhappy that he was farming on his late father's property. In XXXX 2015, he alleges that A. sent armed men to his home. In XXXX 2015, he alleges that A. destroyed crops on the land. The Appellant alleges that he fled Ondo State for Lagos, where he resided in a church. In XXXX 2016, he travelled to Ghana, and he returned to Nigeria.2 After receiving his United States (US) visa in XXXX 2016, he left for the US in XXXX 2016, where he remained for 1.5 years without claiming asylum.3 In XXXX 2018, he entered Canada and initiated his refugee claim.

The RPD rejected the Appellant's claim, finding that he has a viable Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) in Lagos and Port Harcourt. As part of its IFA analysis, the RPD identified a Basis of Claim (BOC) omission about an alleged XXXX 2015 threat from A. that he would come to Lagos to find the Appellant. The RPD also drew negative inferences based on a delay in departure and a failure to claim asylum in the US. The Appellant argues that the RPD decision is incorrect. He has not submitted any new evidence, and I have no jurisdiction to hold a hearing.4

Having independently assessed all the evidence, I find that the overall RPD decision is correct. The RPD was correct to find that the Appellant has a viable IFA in Lagos. As I have found that the Appellant has a viable IFA in Lagos, it is not necessary to determine the correctness of the RPD's finding that Port Harcourt is a viable IFA. The availability of a viable IFA in Lagos is determinative.
I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

I am reviewing the RPD's decision on the standard of correctness as I do not find the RPD enjoyed a meaningful advantage. I have conducted an independent assessment of the evidence to determine whether, as submitted by the Appellant, the RPD erred.5 The Appellant is responsible for raising any potential grounds of appeal that arise from the RPD decision.6 It is not the Refugee Appeal Division's (RAD) role to come up with ideas to assist him in succeeding with his appeal.7 Issues on appeal

The Appellant argues that the RPD erred, as follows: * In finding inconsistencies in his testimony; * In failing to give him sufficient notice about the IFA locations; and * In finding that he has a safe and reasonable IFA in Lagos and Port Harcourt.
Having independently assessed the evidence, I find that the overall RPD decision is correct. Unchallenged RPD finding that the Appellant lacks a nexus is correct

The RPD found that the Appellant's claim lacks a nexus to a Convention ground. 8 Counsel does not identify any error in this finding, and I find none in my independent assessment. The Appellant alleges that his life is at risk based on a property dispute with his uncle. The Appellant has not established a nexus to a Convention ground underlying this alleged risk. I find that the Appellant does not face a serious possibility of persecution by reason of his race, nationality, political opinion, religion, or particular social group, and that there is no nexus to a Convention ground. Having failed to establish a nexus, the Appellant does not have a well-founded fear of persecution under section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). The RPD was correct to draw a negative credibility inference based on the BOC omission

While the RPD accepted the central allegations in the Appellant's claim, it drew negative inferences based on his delay in departure and failure to claim asylum in the US. Counsel argues that the Appellant provided a reasonable explanation for his delayed departure and failure to claim asylum in the US. Specifically, that the Appellant left Nigeria as soon as he could afford his plane fare and that he could not afford a lawyer to assist him with an asylum claim in the US. Delay in departure and failure to claim are rarely determinative of credibility on their own, and the RPD acknowledged that these grounds are not sufficient to find the Appellant wholly lacking in credibility. In my independent assessment, I draw no adverse inference based on the Appellant's delay in leaving Nigeria and his failure to claim protection in the US.

The RPD also identified a BOC omission about an alleged XXXX 2015 threat from A. that he would come to Lagos to find the Appellant.9 Counsel does not identify any error in this finding, and I find none in my independent assessment. The Appellant alleged in testimony that a family member called him in XXXX 2015 to warn him that A. threatened to come and find him in Lagos and kill him.10 This allegation was not included in the initial BOC or amended BOC.11 When confronted with this BOC omission at the RPD hearing, the Appellant explained that he forgot to include this allegation in his BOC.12 When asked why he had failed to mention this allegation when he amended his BOC or at the beginning of the RPD hearing, when he confirmed his BOC was complete, true, and correct,13 the Appellant repeated that he had forgotten.14

The RPD correctly considered and rejected the Appellant's explanation.15 Having independently assessed the entire Record, I do not find that the Appellant's explanation is sufficient. This is not minor or peripheral in nature. Rather, the omission is with respect to a material allegation. Whether or no A. threatened to locate and harm in Lagos goes to the heart of his claim. I find that the RPD was correct to expect the Appellant to provide consistent evidence about this alleged threat. The BOC instructs Claimants to include everything that is important for their claim. The Appellant had the assistance of an interpreter and counsel in preparing his BOC.16 He confirmed under oath that all the information in his BOC was translated to him and that the information in his BOC is complete, true, and correct.17 He also filed a BOC amendment with Counsel which offered no correction.18 In my independent assessment, I find that the RPD's finding about the BOC omission is correct. The affidavit from the family member who allegedly called the Appellant to deliver the warning also does not mention this threat from A.19 The Appellant has failed to credibly establish that A. threatened to locate and harm him in Lagos, as alleged. I draw an adverse credibility inference. While not determinative on its own, the RPD was correct to draw an adverse inference based on this material BOC omission. The Appellant was given sufficient notice of the IFA locations

The RPD notified the Appellant that it was proposing Lagos and Port Harcourt as IFA locations at the beginning of the hearing.20 Counsel argues that the RPD erred when it failed to notify the Appellant of the IFA locations before the hearing.21 Counsel also argues that the RPD erred when it proposed the IFA locations halfway through the hearing.22 I am not persuaded by either of Counsel's arguments. Having independently assessed all the evidence, I find that the RPD provided the Appellant with sufficient notice that it would be considering whether he has a viable IFA in Lagos and Port Harcourt.

First, the RPD is not required to notify Claimants before the hearing that it will be considering an IFA, or which cities it will be proposing. Proper notice of an IFA is given where it is raised at the hearing and a Claimant is given the opportunity to address the issue with evidence and argument.23 The RPD's discussion of IFA at the hearing is sufficient to notify a Claimant of this determinative issue.24 It was open to Counsel to submit an application for post-hearing disclosure about the IFA locations, if she believed this was necessary.25 She did not do so.

Second, Counsel is incorrect that the RPD waited until halfway through the proceedings to propose Lagos and Port Harcourt as IFA locations. The Record indicates that the RPD raised the possibility of an IFA in Lagos and Port Harcourt at the beginning of the hearing before any testimony was taken. 26 The RPD then went on to ask detailed questions about the IFA locations.27 Counsel had every opportunity to ask the Appellant further questions with respect to the IFAs, if she believed additional testimony was necessary. She did not do so.28 The RPD provided clear and sufficient notice that it would be considering the viability of an IFA in Lagos and Port Harcourt. Counsel's argument is without merit. The RPD did not err. The RPD was correct to find that Lagos is a viable IFA

The RPD proposed Lagos and Port Harcourt as viable IFA locations. Once an IFA is proposed, it is the Claimant's burden to adduce evidence to show, on a balance of probabilities: (i) that they face a serious possibility of persecution or a subsection 97(1) risk in the IFA; or (ii) that it would be objectively unreasonable, in their personal circumstances, to relocate to the IFA.29 It is not the RPD's job to prove or establish that the IFA location is safe or reasonable; the burden is on the Claimant.30 The RPD found that the Appellant has a viable IFA in Lagos and Port Harcourt. Having independently assessed all the evidence, and carefully considered the arguments on appeal, I find that the RPD decision is correct. I find that the Appellant has a viable IFA in Lagos. As I have found that the Appellant has a viable IFA in Lagos, it is not necessary for me to determine the correctness of the RPD's finding that Port Harcourt is also a viable IFA. The availability of an IFA location in Lagos is determinative. No serious possibility of persecution, or subsection 97(1) risk, in the IFA location

The RPD found that the Appellant failed to establish his claim under the first prong of the IFA test.31 Counsel argues that this finding is in error. I disagree. Having independently assessed the evidence, I find that the Appellant has failed to establish that the agent of harm possesses the means and motivation32 to locate him in Lagos, such that he faces a serious possibility of persecution or subsection 97(1) risk.

Counsel argues that the concept of an IFA is an "antiquated concept in today's world" and that in finding an IFA is viable, the RPD is "confining the [A]ppellant[] to one city for the rest of their lives."33 I disagree. It is trite law that "the concept of an IFA is an inherent part of the Convention refugee definition."34 Counsel also argues that the prevalence of social media in Nigeria defeats the first prong of the IFA test.35 Counsel's argument that someone else could take a photograph of the Appellant and post it to social media, thereby alerting the agent of harm, is speculative. Moreover, the Appellant does not allege a public profile on social media and has not tendered evidence of such a profile on social media before the RPD or before me on appeal. As the Federal Court found in Ohwofasa, the mere allegation without more that social media provides a means for an agent of persecution to locate a Claimant "is no more than speculative, at best, far from a serious possibility."36 I do not find it unreasonable for the Appellant to keep social media posts private. The Federal Court has found that the requirement to keep social media posts private is not akin to requiring a Claimant to live in hiding.37

Counsel also argues that the Appellant is at risk due to corruption and the availability of databases administered by the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) and the National Communication Commission (NCC).38 Having independently assessed all the evidence, I disagree.

The information in the National Documentation Package (NDP) for Nigeria does not support the Appellant's assertion that the information in the CBN could be used by his agent of harm to locate him. The NDP states: According to the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN)'s Regulatory Framework for Bank Verification Number (BVN) Operations and Watch-List for the Nigerian Banking Industry [...] the following entities can access BVN information, subject to the approval of the CBN [RAD's Note: Central Bank of Nigeria]: DMBs [Deposit Money Banks], OFIs [other financial institutions], MMOs [Mobile Money Operators], PSPs [Payment Service Providers], law enforcement agencies, credit bureaus and "[o]ther entities as applicable" (CBN 18 Oct. 2017, 8-9). In July 2018, media sources reported that section 1.6 of the CBN's framework for access to BVN information was amended to add the requirement of obtaining a "'valid [c]ourt [o]rder'" before the disclosure of BVN information (Daily Post 13 July 2018; Business Post 15 July 2018). 39

While the Appellant has provided supporting evidence that alleges that A. is an ex-soldier,40 he has not established that A. has any connection that can be used to access the CBN database. The Appellant failed to present any evidence that the agent of harm has access to security agents to retrieve this data or that he is sufficiently influential to gain access through some other means. The Appellant is speculating without an evidentiary foundation. While the facts alleged by the Appellant is presumed truthful, this presumption does not apply to belief or speculation.41 Mere speculation is insufficient to establish a fact, on a balance of probabilities.

The NDP also does not support the Appellant's claim that the NCC database could be used to locate him in the IFA location. The NDP states: The Nigerian Communications Commission (Registration of Telephone Subscribers) Regulations, 2011 provides that the information of mobile telephone subscribers registered in the central database can only be provided to security agencies and that the request must be made in writing by "an official of the requesting Security Agency who is not below the rank of an Assistant Commissioner of Police or a coordinate rank of any other Security Agency" (Nigeria 2011, Art. 8). According to the same source, mobile telephone service providers must obtain the subscriber's written consent before disclosing their personal information to a third party, excluding security agencies (Nigeria 2011, Art. 10). However, sources report that, according to the head of the NCC's Projects Department, "the Office of the National Security Adviser (ONSA) has a direct link to" the NCC's SIM card registration database in order to facilitate the monitoring and apprehension of criminals (Daily Trust 6 Mar. 2018; TechCity 8 Mar. 2018).42
The Appellant failed to present any evidence that the agent of harm has access to security agents to retrieve this data or that he is sufficiently influential to gain access through other means.

The Appellant fled Ondo State in XXXX 2015, nearly 7 years ago. He has not credibly established that any threats from his agent of harm have occurred since this time. In addition, Lagos is nearly 250 kilometres away from the Appellant's hometown in Ondo State.43 It is also a large city with a population of 14.86 million people.44 While not determinative, the population of a proposed IFA, as well as its distance from a Claimant's home city, are relevant factors to be considered.45 The objective evidence indicates that where a person fears non-state agents, relocation to another area of Nigeria is likely to be generally viable.46

The Appellant bears the onus to show that he does not have a viable IFA. The fact that he believes that he is at risk in the IFA location does not make it so, and it does not discharge his burden. Having independently assessed all the evidence, I find that the Appellant has not established that his agent of harm possesses the means or motivation to locate him in Lagos, such that he faces a serious possibility of persecution, or a subsection 97(1) risk, in the IFA location. The IFA location is objectively reasonable in the Appellant's circumstances

The RPD found that Lagos is an objectively reasonable IFA in the Appellant's personal circumstances.47 Counsel argues that this finding is incorrect. I disagree. Having reviewed the entire Record, I find that the RPD was correct, and that Lagos is an objectively reasonable IFA.

The RPD considered that the Appellant is Christian and that he has over a decade of work experience in the XXXX industry as well as 3 years of post-secondary education completed in English.48 The RPD correctly applied these circumstances to the areas of employment and indigeneship, finding that the Appellant failed to establish that it would be objectively unreasonable for him to relocate to Lagos.

In my independent assessment, I have considered the Appellant's personal circumstances in determining the viability of Lagos as an IFA location. I have considered the Appellant's ability to travel safely to Lagos and remain there without facing undue hardship. The reasonableness of an IFA location is to be objectively established.49 The threshold for the objectively unreasonable standard is very high and requires, at a minimum, actual, and concrete evidence of adverse conditions which would jeopardize the Appellant's life and safety.50 I find that the Appellant has not established that his relocation to the IFA in Lagos would be objectively unreasonable, in consideration of his personal circumstances. i. Employment and accommodation in Lagos

I acknowledge the difficulties that the Appellant may face in finding employment and accommodation in Lagos. However, when the Appellant's personal circumstances are considered, specifically the Appellant's education and employment experience, I find that his relocation to Lagos is not unreasonable.

The Appellant is a 48 year old man who has completed 14 years of education, which places him in the upper half of Nigerian men in terms of educational achievement.51 The objective evidence indicates that on average Nigerian men have 9 years of formal education while the Appellant has 14 years, with 3 of those years completed in a post-secondary institution.52 The Appellant also has over a decade of experience in the XXXX industry.53 I find that the Appellant's education and employment experience will assist him in obtaining employment and housing in Lagos. I acknowledge that "people relocating in Nigeria, including non-natives, would not benefit from government assistance."54 I also acknowledge the difficulty in locating employment and the high cost of housing and food in Lagos. However, "'[i]n most cosmopolitan and urban Nigerian cities, issues of indigeneity [are] ... nonexistent' and it is mostly at the local government level, in the 'political arena,' and particularly when it comes to sharing resources, that indigeneity becomes an issue."55 In Lagos, "jobs are not reserved for Lagos indigenes" and non-indigenes are not required to establish their state of origin or indigeneity before accessing public services, civil service jobs, or university posts.56 While there will be uncertainty in the process of finding work and housing in a new city, I do not find that this meets the high threshold required to demonstrate that relocating to the IFA would be objectively unreasonable in the Appellant's circumstances.

The hardship caused by an inability to locate suitable work, loss of employment, loss of status, reduction in quality of life, loss of aspirations, loss of beloved ones, and frustration of one's expectations alone does not meet the high threshold under the second prong of the test.57 I find it reasonable that someone of the Appellant's age, education, and experience would be able to obtain employment in the IFA location in order to secure housing and financially support himself and his wife and children, who already reside in Lagos. ii. Religion, language, ethnicity, and transport in Lagos

The Appellant is Christian, and he speaks English.58 While the Appellant had the assistance of a Yoruba language interpreter when completing his BOC and at his refugee hearing, he completed 3 years of post-secondary education in English. The official language of Nigeria is English, and Pidgin English is widely spoken in Lagos.59 While religious conflict in the North and Middle Belt of Nigeria is common,60 the situation for Christians in Lagos State is "'normal'", they "live 'peacefully' along with people of other religions", and there are only isolated occurrences of religious violence.61

Having independently assessed all the evidence, I acknowledge that discrimination against non-indigenes can be a problem in Nigeria. Non-indigenes can face discrimination in seeking government employment, political office, and in accessing some government services.62 Relocation may be more difficult for non-indigenes without access to support.63 In Lagos, "there are occasional indigene-settler issues" but the city "has a long history of accommodating non-indigenes."64 Indigeneship status is less significant in large urban centres, such as Lagos, given that "all large cities have quite large migrant communities from other parts of the country."65 Lagos is also dominated by the Appellant's own ethnic group, the Yoruba.66 Even where his status as a non-indigene will pose difficulties for the Appellant in Lagos, I am not satisfied that this meets the high threshold required to demonstrate that the IFA is objectively unreasonable in his circumstances.

Finally, I disagree with Counsel's argument that the Appellant would be unable to relocate and move freely. Lagos is serviced by an international airport which the Appellant could use to travel safely to the IFA location.67 IFA summary

Having considered the totality or cumulative effect of the Appellant's personal circumstances, I find that the IFA location is viable. I am mindful that my role is to consider the totality or cumulative effect of the Appellant's personal circumstances to determine whether an IFA location is reasonable. I find that the proposed IFA is not unreasonable in consideration of the Appellant's particular circumstances on an individual or cumulative basis. I acknowledge the difficulties of relocating. However, the threshold for unreasonableness is high and "requires nothing less than the existence of conditions which would jeopardize the life and safety of a claimant."68 Having independently assessed all the evidence, I find that Lagos is a viable IFA.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. (signed) J. Pollock J.
